cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low risk — Municipal splits and recombinations from 1970 to 2000 are harmonized into constant-boundary Minimum Comparable Areas (MCAs) using decennial census universes, with only a handful of localities having fewer than 10 surveyed small houses excluded.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious risk — Urban-area fixed effects, lagged covariates, spatial lag/error MLE, and 2SLS/LIML (instrumenting water servicing with porous geology and insolation interactions and housing supply with 1970 census/market-access variables) address major endogeneity, but plausible IV exclusion-restriction violations (geology/rivers affecting private water costs or growth amenities; persistent unobserved locality fundamentals), modest multi-endogenous first-stage strength (partial F ~ 13; F = 6.2 for untitled homes), and spatial weight-matrix sensitivity leave substantial residual confounding risk.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate — Although the institutional narrative accurately describes Brazil's 1979 federal 125 sq m minimum lot-size statute, pre-1988 legal bars on municipal infrastructure provision in informal favelas and loteamentos, and 1999/2005 IBGE municipal zoning surveys, the econometric models do not directly code municipal legal rules or utility refusal ordinances over time, relying instead on realized census water connection shares among small houses as an indirect proxy for exclusionary policy.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Serious risk for exposure / Low risk for outcomes — Exclusionary municipal policy is not observed directly and is proxied ecologically by the census share of 1–3 room houses connected to a central water network (which conflates intentional exclusion with capacity backlogs and non-migrant small dwellings), whereas demographic growth and household piped-water connection outcomes come from standardized IBGE Population Censuses.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Strong — Household counts, household-head educational attainment, central piped water connections, and full servicing (electricity, central water, and central sewerage) are measured consistently across localities from official decennial IBGE Population Censuses (1970, 1980, 1991, 2000), though water quality, service intermittency, and affordability/tariffs are not observed.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate risk (no pre-analysis plan) — No pre-registration or protocol exists for this 2008 NBER working paper, and the text reports specification choices guided by specification tests (including selecting the 1991–2000 growth window over 1980–1991, choosing distance-to-Sao-Paulo and geology/insolation instrument lists based on strength and orthogonality tests, and favoring inverse-density weights where inverse-distance weights were insignificant); additionally, end-of-paper table/figure pages (PDF pp. 39–46, 48, 50) are unextracted in the PDF text.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate risk — The main econometric sample includes 351 harmonized MCAs across 55 multi-locality urban areas that were at least 50% urbanized at baseline, avoiding post-treatment selection on outcomes, though restricting to baseline-urbanized localities in multi-locality agglomerations excludes initially rural fringe municipalities (<50% urban at baseline) experiencing rapid informal settlement growth.

domain_ratings.justification: In Section 4 (strategic servicing regressions), identification relies on urban-area fixed effects, 1980 lagged covariates (OLS), and spatial autoregressive/error MLE, because instruments for competitors' servicing (W'b) were unacceptably weak; results are sensitive to spatial weight specification (insignificant with inverse-distance weights) and vulnerable to unobserved intra-metropolitan fiscal or topographic cost differences. In Section 5 (1991–2000 household growth and composition), 2SLS and LIML use porous geology interacted with insolation and 1970 historical census/market-access instruments alongside urban-area fixed effects, but the authors explicitly acknowledge exclusion-restriction concerns (geology and rivers may affect contemporaneous private water costs or local amenities; 1970 historical instruments require broken persistence in locality unobservables) and modest multi-endogenous first-stage strength (partial F around 13 in main models and 6.2 when using untitled houses).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: Units of analysis are harmonized Minimum Comparable Areas (MCAs) constructed from 1970–2000 Brazilian Population Censuses (351 MCAs in 55 multi-locality urban areas with >=50% urban population in the base period, dropping a handful of small localities with <10 surveyed small houses). Conditioning on baseline urbanization (>=50% in 1980 or 1991) avoids conditioning on post-intervention growth, and dropping the 25 most fragmented multi-municipality MCAs leaves results unchanged; however, excluding localities <50% urban at baseline omits initially rural peripheral municipalities undergoing rapid suburban/informal expansion.

domain_ratings.justification: Although framed around intentional municipal exclusionary policy enabled by pre-1988 legal restrictions on servicing informal settlements (favelas and loteamentos violating the 1979 national 125 sq m minimum lot-size law), the study does not directly measure municipal exclusionary rules or utility denial policies. Instead, it proxies exclusionary policy via the realized 1991 census share of all small houses (1–3 rooms) connected to a central water system. Only 33% of migrants (and 18% of non-migrants) lived in 1–3 room homes in 1991, and low water coverage also reflects non-strategic infrastructure backlogs from rapid prior growth or regional utility constraints. A closer proxy (water connections among untitled owner-occupied homes) lacked 1980 data and yielded weak instruments (partial F = 6.2) and imprecise estimates.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1 (PDF pp. 5–6); Section 2.3–2.4 (PDF pp. 9–13); Section 4.1 (PDF p. 22); Section 5 & 5.2.1 (PDF pp. 29, 33)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: Section 5 estimates the effect of 1991 baseline small-house water servicing (shaped during the pre-1988 non-democratic period) on 1991–2000 locality growth. Following the 1988 Constitution and democratization, national and local governments removed bans on servicing informal settlements, launched widespread slum-upgrading and land-regularization programs, and enacted new municipal minimum lot-size laws (>125 sq m) during the 1990s. These concurrent 1991–2000 policy shifts and upgrading co-interventions are not directly controlled for in the growth regressions.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Feler and Henderson (2008) conduct a non-randomized comparative longitudinal/panel econometric evaluation across 351 urban Minimum Comparable Areas (MCAs) in 55 multi-locality Brazilian urban areas (1970–2000 IBGE Censuses), examining (1) strategic municipal under-provision of central piped water to small (1–3 room) houses in 1991 using urban-area fixed effects, lagged OLS, and spatial lag/error MLE, and (2) the causal effect of 1991 small-house water servicing on 1991–2000 urban household growth and educational composition using 2SLS and LIML instrumental variables (porous geology, insolation interactions, and 1970 historical census/market-access variables). Appraised with ROBINS-I, overall risk of bias is Serious, driven by two Serious-risk domains: D1 (Confounding) and D3 (Classification of interventions). Specifically, deliberate exclusionary policy is not directly measured from municipal ordinances or utility refusal records but is proxied ecologically by census piped-water coverage among all 1–3 room dwellings (which conflates intentional exclusion with rapid-growth infrastructure backlogs); furthermore, in the IV growth regressions, geological and historical 1970 instruments face plausible exclusion-restriction violations and only modest multi-endogenous first-stage strength (partial F ~ 13, dropping to 6.2 when water coverage of untitled homes is used), while spatial reaction-function estimates are sensitive to weight-matrix specification. Strengths include harmonized MCA boundaries preventing municipal-split attrition (Low risk in D5), standardized decennial census outcome measurement (Low risk in D6), and informative falsification checks (1991 large houses and post-democratization 2000 small houses). Note that in the provided PDF text extraction, full prose is available on PDF pp. 1–38 and 47, whereas end-of-paper table/figure pages (PDF pp. 39–46, 48, 50) are blank/unextracted.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Non-randomized comparative longitudinal/panel econometric policy evaluation using spatial reaction-function regressions (lagged OLS and spatial autoregressive/error MLE) and instrumental-variables (2SLS and LIML) regressions with urban-area fixed effects across harmonized Brazilian localities (1970–2000 decennial censuses)

raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study evaluates the determinants and causal population-growth/composition impacts of municipal public water-servicing policy across Brazilian localities over 1980–2000 using comparative panel/longitudinal fixed-effects regressions, spatial reaction models, and 2SLS/LIML instrumental variables. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, non-randomized comparative longitudinal/panel and instrumental-variables policy evaluations map directly to ROBINS-I.
